food.text: Of the 70 to 120 million people who died in famines worldwide during the 20th century, over half died in China. An estimated 30 million died in the famine of 1958 to 1961 alone, making it the deadliest of the century.

Chinese cooking travelled abroad through emigrants, and Cantonese chefs became highly sought after throughout China. Until the late 20th century, most Chinese restaurants in the West served largely Cantonese dishes.

In 2011, UNESCO declared Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan Province, a city of gastronomy. Sichuan cuisine is renowned for fiery and bold tastes, from liberal use of garlic and chilis and the unique flavors of Sichuan pepper. Kung Pao chicken and Yuxiang shredded pork are examples.

Chinese restaurants in the United States adapted dishes to local tastes, so American Chinese food often differs from styles common in China. By the late 20th century it was recognized as one of the regional styles of Chinese cuisine.

American Chinese cuisine has its roots in immigrants from Guangdong province, particularly the Toisan (Taishan) district, the origin of most Chinese immigration before immigration was closed in 1924. Among China's regional cuisines, Cantonese cuisine had the most influence on American Chinese food.

In 1936, a severe drought in Sichuan, worsened by the ongoing civil war, led to a famine that killed up to five million people and caused large-scale cannibalism. Human flesh became a traded commodity, with a higher black-market price charged for fresh flesh from a person killed for food than for flesh from a corpse.
The famine of 1942 to 1943 hit Henan during the Japanese invasion of China. Ecological disasters combined with war pressures led to mass starvation, and widespread cannibalism occurred there again.

Chinese restaurants became part of Jewish life in New York City. By 1936, at least 18 Chinese tea gardens and restaurants operated in heavily Jewish neighborhoods like the Lower East Side. In 1935, a restaurant owner named Eng Shee Chuck brought chow mein on Christmas Day to the Jewish Children's Home in Newark. Before the emancipation of the Jews in Europe, Christmas had been a dangerous holiday for Jews, a night of drunken violence and sometimes pogroms, so they stayed home for their safety.
Severe famine struck Henan, Hubei and Anhui after the 1931 Chinese floods. Officials, relief workers and missionaries reported that it led to cannibalism in rural areas.
Chinese chef William Wing Young developed the dim sim, or "dimmy", around 1945 in Melbourne. Inspired by dim sum, it is a dumpling with thick crispy skin filled with meat and is usually fried.

art.text: The China Pavilion of Expo 2010 in Shanghai was the tallest structure at the Expo, at 63 metres, and the most expensive pavilion, costing an estimated US$220 million. It is nicknamed "the Crown of the East" because it resembles an ancient crown.

Neo-Chinese style is a late-20th and early 21st-century movement that combines traditional Chinese elements with modern culture in architecture, creative arts and fashion. In fashion it gained popularity in the 2020s, reflecting the younger generation's identification and confidence with Chinese culture.

Throughout the 20th century, Chinese architects tried to bring traditional Chinese designs into modern architecture. Urban development pressure reduced demand for traditional buildings, which are normally under 3 levels, in favor of high-rises.
Architect He Jingtang led the team that designed the China Pavilion. They drew inspiration from the Chinese corbel bracket called dougong and from the ancient bronze cauldron called ding.

After Expo 2010, the pavilion became a museum. The China Art Museum, Shanghai opened there on 1 October 2012, China's National Day, and the building is more than ten times larger than the museum's previous home.

In Chinese architecture, Chinese cultural elements were combined with neoclassical architecture in the 1950s. Modern architecture was combined with postmodernism from the late 1980s, helping create neo-Chinese architecture.

The Shanghai Art Museum was established in 1956 in a former restaurant on West Nanjing Road. On 18 March 2000 it moved into the former Shanghai Race Club building on People's Square, which had housed the Shanghai Library until 1997.

The Urban Future Pavilion from Expo 2010 was converted into the Power Station of Art, a municipal museum for contemporary art. It opened on 1 October 2012, the same day as the China Art Museum, Shanghai.
In neo-Chinese fashion, simplified traditional elements are joined with modern designs. One example is the Mandarin collar, which appears in contemporary shirts and dresses.
From 1952 to 1954, socialist realism from the Soviet Union influenced Chinese architecture. Modernism and the Chinese national style were other major trends in that period.
The exhibition "The Picturesque China" ran for a year and showed 21st-century artworks by more than 260 Chinese artists. It was divided into five units and ended on 30 September 2013.

war.text: The Second Sino-Japanese War, fought between the Republic of China and the Empire of Japan from 1937 to 1945, was the largest Asian war of the 20th century. It is often regarded as the beginning of World War II in Asia, as it became heavily intertwined with the wider conflict after Japan attacked the United States. The war killed around 20 million people, mostly Chinese civilians. Japan carried out the largest attacks in the history of biological warfare, causing at least 200,000 deaths, and used chemical weapons including lethal blister agents.

The Chinese Civil War between the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party began on 1 August 1927, after the Kuomintang purged communists in the Shanghai massacre of 12 April 1927 through hundreds of arrests and executions, and it ended with the Kuomintang's retreat to Taiwan on 7 December 1949. Fighting was mostly put on hold from 1937 to 1945 while both sides faced the Japanese invasion, though armed clashes between them remained common. In the New Fourth Army incident, Kuomintang forces ambushed the Communist New Fourth Army, which led to several thousand deaths and ended the Second United Front.

In February 1979, Chinese forces launched a surprise invasion of northern Vietnam and quickly captured several cities near the border. Lạng Sơn fell on 6 March after three days of bloody house-to-house fighting, and the Chinese took Mong Cai but suffered heavy casualties. China declared its punitive mission accomplished on 6 March and withdrew, using a scorched-earth policy that destroyed local infrastructure and looted equipment and livestock, severely weakening the economy of Vietnam's northernmost provinces. The offensive was ostensibly a response to Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia in 1978.

The Sino-Indian War lasted from October to November 1962 and was fought in two places roughly 1,000 km apart: the North-East Frontier Agency and the Aksai Chin region. India recognised the Johnson Line in the west and the McMahon Line in the east, while China did not recognise them.

In late 1933, Chiang Kai-shek encircled the Chinese Communists to try to destroy them, forcing them into the Long March. The Communists lost around 90% of their men. As a Japanese invasion became imminent, Chiang formed a United Front with them in 1936, a process hastened by the Xi'an Incident.

The 1962 conflict followed a series of border skirmishes after the 1959 Tibetan uprising, when India granted asylum to the 14th Dalai Lama. China's construction of a strategic road through Aksai Chin further escalated the dispute.

The Battle of the Paracel Islands was fought between the Chinese and South Vietnamese navies from 19 to 20 January 1974. China won, and 18 Chinese sailors were killed and 67 wounded. On the South Vietnamese side, 75 soldiers were killed and 16 wounded, and the Chinese took 48 prisoners. China occupied the portion formerly controlled by South Vietnam and established full de facto control over the Paracels.

In late 1967, Chinese and Indian forces clashed twice in Sikkim, in the "Nathu La" and "Cho La" clashes. In both, advancing Chinese forces were forced to withdraw from Sikkim. In 2020, soldiers were killed in skirmishes for the first time since the 1962 war ended.

On 17 February 1917, the German U-boat SM U-65 sank the French passenger/cargo ship SS Athos, which carried 900 Chinese workers. 543 of them were killed, more than half of those aboard. China severed diplomatic ties with Germany in March, and officially declared war on the Central Powers on 14 August 1917.

During the Battle of the Paracel Islands, the South Vietnamese reported that the warship Nhật Tảo was sunk, and 75 South Vietnamese soldiers, including its captain Ngụy Văn Thà, were killed and 16 wounded. On 20 January 1974, the Dutch tanker Kopionella found and rescued 23 survivors of the sunken ship. On 29 January, South Vietnamese fishermen found 15 more soldiers who had fought on Quang Hòa island and escaped in lifeboats.

literature.text: Around the turn of the 20th century, the author Lu Xun (1881-1936) became an influential voice of vernacular Chinese literature. Vernacular writing had matured in novels during the Ming and Qing, but Literary Chinese, patterned on the language of the classics, had long held preeminence.
Gao Xingjian became the first Chinese writer to receive the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2000. He lived in France but continued to write primarily in Chinese. Mo Yan received the same prize in 2012.
As of June 2023, 528 million people in China, 49% of the country's internet users, read internet literature. More than 36 million works of internet literature were available in China as of 2023.

In the 1930s Ba Jin produced a trilogy depicting the struggle of modern youth against the age-old dominance of the Confucian family system. Jia (Family), one of its novels, is often compared with Dream of the Red Chamber.

Mao Dun (1896-1981) was the first of the novelists to emerge from the League of Left-Wing Writers. His work reflected the revolutionary struggle and disillusionment of the late 1920s. Other major writers of the period included Guo Moruo and the satirist Lao She.

According to a 2014 report from the International Publishing Association, China is the largest publisher of books, magazines and newspapers in the world by volume. In 2005 alone, some 128,800 new book titles were published, and there are more than 600 literary journals across the country.
tags: General Administration of Press and Publication

literature.text: Jinjiang Literature City was first established as a platform for pirated Taiwanese novels. In 2003 it began to host original works and grew into one of the largest online literature platforms in China. At the peak of Under the Banyan Tree in 2005, the portal had 4.5 million registered users.

Ba Jin (1904-2005) wrote novels influenced by Ivan Turgenev and other Russian writers. Later, most of the authors of his generation who were still alive during the Cultural Revolution (1966-76) were either purged or forced to submit to public humiliation.

In 2015, children's author Cao Wenxuan was awarded the Hans Christian Andersen Award. He was the first Chinese author to win the top international children's book prize, although several Chinese authors had previously been nominated.

Qidian, launched in 2006, quickly overtook Under the Banyan Tree as a popular online literature site by focusing on marketing and reader engagement. It was among the first to launch a freemium model. In 2004 Shanda Interactive Entertainment acquired Qidian, and in 2008 it acquired Hongxiu and Jinjiang Literature City to create Shanda Literature.
Of the 309 most popular television dramas and films in 2018 and 2019, 21% were adapted from internet literature. Mythical fantasies are among the most popular sources for digital games.

science.text: The Chinese Academy of Sciences is the world's largest research organization, with 106 research institutes, 2 universities, 71,300 full-time employees and 79,000 graduate students. It ranked first in the 2025 SCImago Institutions Rankings. Its historical roots lie in the Academia Sinica of the Republican era.

In 1964, the Chinese Academy of Sciences debuted China's first self-developed large digital computer, the 119. It was a core technology in facilitating China's first successful nuclear weapon test, Project 596, which took place in the same year.

Science and technology in the People's Republic of China developed rapidly from the 1980s to the 2020s. The government launched the 863 Program and the "Strategy to Revitalize the Country Through Science and Education" in the 1980s and 1990s. In 2025, China ranked 10th in the Global Innovation Index.

Joseph Needham began the book series Science and Civilisation in China in 1954, published by Cambridge University Press. It has reached seven volumes in twenty-seven books. The series was named to the Modern Library Board's 100 Best Nonfiction books of the 20th century.

The Chinese Academy of Sciences has created hundreds of commercial enterprises. Lenovo is one of the most famous, and others include Sugon and GoLaxy. The academy also runs two universities of its own.

China's 2006 to 2020 Medium and Long-Term Plan set a target of spending 2.5% of GDP on research and development by 2020. Between 2003 and 2012, spending rose from 1.13% to 1.98% of GDP. This suggested the country was on track to meet its target.

Joseph Needham returned to Cambridge in 1948 and began working with Wang Ling, a Chinese medical student he had met there. Needham first planned a single volume but later proposed up to eleven. After his death in 1995, the Needham Research Institute was established to continue the work.

The University of Science and Technology of China was founded in Beijing by the Chinese Academy of Sciences in September 1958, with Guo Moruo as its first president. It moved to Hefei in 1970 during the Cultural Revolution. In 1959 it became the youngest national key university.

science.text: Membership of the Chinese Academy of Sciences is a lifelong honor and, under bylaws adopted in 1992, the highest academic title in China. Members older than 80 become senior members and may no longer hold leading positions. Academicians can give suggestions and influence state policy on science and technology.

In 2015, China devoted only 5.1% of its research spending to basic research, and enterprises contributed 77% of total research and development expenditure. Enterprises put as much as 97% of their research spending into experimental development. China aimed to raise basic research to 15% of spending by 2020.

The Nature Index Research Leaders 2025 ranked the University of Science and Technology of China first in China and the Asia-Pacific region, and second in the world after Harvard. The ranking measures papers published in 145 leading high-quality science journals.

science.text: Founded in 1978 as the Graduate School of the University of Science and Technology of China, the institution now called the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences was the first graduate school in China. It produced the country's first doctoral graduate in science, first in engineering, and first female doctoral graduate. It became an independent university in 2012.

politics.text: The weak response of the Chinese government to the Treaty of Versailles sparked a surge in nationalism. On 4 May 1919, widespread student protests began in Beijing, involving young students, the general public, business people and other classes, through demonstrations, petitions, strikes and violent confrontations with the government. Support followed from students and workers in Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou and other cities. The Chinese delegation was the only one that did not sign the treaty at the ceremony.

The Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek and the Communists under Mao Zedong had fought each other in the Chinese Civil War since 1927. After Chiang encircled the Communists in late 1933, the Long March followed, and the Communists lost around 90% of their men. Facing a Japanese invasion, Chiang formed a United Front with them in 1936, hastened by the Xi'an Incident.

The Century of Humiliation is a concept for the period from the end of the First Opium War to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. Both the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party popularized it in the 1920s. It has since been invoked in incidents such as the Hainan Island incident and the 2008 Beijing Olympics torch relay protests.

Historians usually mark the abdication of the Xuantong Emperor, Puyi, on 12 February 1912 as the end of the Chinese dynastic system. Later attempts to revive monarchy, including the Manchu Restoration of 1917, which lasted merely 11 days, are not regarded as legitimate continuations.

When Yuan Shikai became emperor, he took the era name Hongxian, meaning "Promote the constitution". He planned for 1916 to be "Hongxian Year 1" instead of "Republic Year 5", but his own subordinate military commanders opposed him. They believed monarchy would let him rule without depending on the military's support.

In January 1915, Japan issued the Twenty-One Demands to China, including Japanese control of former German rights and 99-year leases in southern Manchuria. Yuan Shikai, competing with warlords to rule all China, could not risk war with Japan and accepted appeasement. The final treaty was signed on 25 May 1915.

China ended its neutrality on 14 August 1917, declaring war on Germany and Austria-Hungary. This followed the sinking of the French ship SS Athos by a German U-boat on 17 February 1917, which killed 543 of the 900 Chinese workers aboard. Premier Duan Qirui spearheaded the move, hoping to integrate China with Europe and the United States. China never sent troops overseas, but 140,000 labourers served the British and French forces; the number of Chinese who died in the war is unknown, with European records saying 2,000 and Chinese scholars up to 20,000, most from the Spanish flu but others from shelling, landmines and poor treatment.

On 18 September 1931, the Japanese staged the Mukden incident, a false flag event fabricated to justify invading Manchuria. Kwantung Army soldiers set off a bomb on the South Manchuria Railway to provoke an opportunity to act in "self defense". Japan then occupied all of Manchuria after five months of fighting and established the puppet state of Manchukuo.

After Japan captured Wuhan in 1938, China's de facto capital at the time, the Nationalist government relocated to Chongqing in the interior. Both sides suffered tremendous casualties in the battle, the Chinese losing up to 500,000 soldiers killed or wounded and the Japanese up to 200,000. To overcome Chinese resistance, Japanese forces frequently deployed poison gas and committed atrocities against civilians, such as a "mini-Nanjing Massacre" in the city of Jiujiang upon its capture.

In 1943, the major western Allied nations agreed, at the direction of the United States, to revoke all unequal treaties they had signed with the Qing government. This officially ended the Treaty System and foreign extraterritoriality, making foreign nationals subject to Chinese laws.

After the Qing dynasty fell, the last emperor Puyi lived in the Forbidden City until 1924, when he moved to the Japanese concession in Tianjin. In 1932 the Empire of Japan invaded Northeast China and founded Manchukuo there, with Puyi as its emperor. Manchukuo fell in 1945, after the Soviet Union invaded Northeast China to fight Japan.

Local governments' documents from the Cultural Revolution (1966 to 1976) revealed hundreds of incidents of cannibalism for ideological reasons rather than hunger, including large-scale cannibalism during the Guangxi Massacre. Cannibal acts occurred at public events organized by local Communist Party officials, with people taking part to prove their revolutionary passion. The writer Zheng Yi documented many of these incidents, especially those in Guangxi, in his 1993 book, Scarlet Memorial.

Although the country's name in Chinese was changed to the Empire of China for state matters, it continued to be officially called the Republic of China in English. Yuan's Ritual Regulations Office also changed the anthem's lyrics in December 1915, replacing "Five Races Under One Union" with a reference to the abdication system of Yao and Shun.

philosophy.text: Since 1949 China has been ruled by the Chinese Communist Party, which officially espouses state atheism, has conducted antireligious campaigns to this end, and prohibits party members from religious practice while in office. The government formally recognizes only five religions: Buddhism, Taoism, Catholicism, Protestantism and Islam. Freedom of religion is substantially curtailed.

In the early 20th century, Chinese intellectuals blamed Confucianism for the scientific and political backwardness of China, after disastrous conflicts with Western military technology at the dawn of the modern era.

Marxist philosophy was imported into China between 1900 and 1930, in translations from German, Russian and Japanese. Ma Junwu, the Chinese translator of Darwin's The Origin of Species, was also the first to introduce Marxism into China. For him, evolutionism and Marxism were the secrets of social development.

Mao Zedong developed his own sinified version of dialectical materialism, drawing on Soviet Marxism-Leninism while centering it on concepts like practice and contradiction. After the Communist victory in 1949, Maoism became the dominant state ideological system. Previous schools of thought were denounced as backward, and later purged during the Cultural Revolution as part of the campaign against the Four Olds. Mao Zedong Thought remains one of the Communist Party's guiding ideologies.

A 2012 survey by the China Family Panel Studies, published in 2014, found that only 12.6% of China's population belongs to its five state-sanctioned religious groups. Only 6.3% of the rest are atheists, while the remaining 81% pray to or worship gods and ancestors in the manner of traditional popular religion.

The Cultural Revolution (1966-1976), the culmination of a series of anti-religious campaigns, involved a systematic effort to destroy religion. It destroyed many places of worship and forced many observances and religious organisations underground. After Mao's death, later leaders allowed Chinese religious organisations more autonomy, and in the 1980s and 1990s the central government began rebuilding the places of worship that had been destroyed.

Chinese dialectical materialism began to be formalized in the 1930s under the influence of Mitin's New Philosophy. Li Da translated many early works of German social democracy and Soviet Marxism into Chinese, and Ai Siqi translated many of Mitin's works and helped introduce the New Philosophy to China.

In the 1980s the Dengist reforms led to large-scale translation of works of Western Marxism and Marxist Humanism into Chinese. Before that, Maoist Dialectics had remained the dominant paradigm into the 1970s, and most debates were on technical questions of dialectical ontology.

After the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, governments and modernizing elites condemned popular religion as "feudal superstition", and most temples were turned to other uses or destroyed. The government of modern China generally tolerates popular religious movements, but has suppressed or persecuted large organizations it fears would undermine social stability.

In Mao's 1964 Talk on Questions of Philosophy, he rejected any possibility of synthesizing divided opposites. He saw the struggle between opposites as the key to dialectics, and this played a major role in the One Divides Into Two controversy of the 1960s.

culture.text: A 2012 survey published in 2014 found that only 12.6% of China's population belongs to one of its five state-sanctioned religious groups. Of the rest, only 6.3% are atheists, while about 81% (1 billion people) pray to or worship gods and ancestors in the traditional popular manner.

At the start of the 20th century, most Chinese people were illiterate, and the many regional languages prevented spoken communication between areas. Reformers chose Beijing-based Mandarin as the national spoken language. After the May 4th Movement, Classical Chinese was quickly replaced by written vernacular Chinese modeled on the standard spoken language.

After the Qing dynasty fell in 1911, governments and modernizing elites condemned "feudal superstition" and opposed traditional religious practices they felt conflicted with modern values. After the Xinhai Revolution most temples were turned to other uses or destroyed, and the Nationalist government's 1928 policy tried to abolish the cults of nearly all gods. By the late 20th century these attitudes began to change, and many scholars now view folk religion in a positive light.

In 1958 the Ministry of Culture held a meeting to launch a Great Leap Forward in cinema. The film industry expanded rapidly, with documentaries growing the most. The number of screening venues, including urban cinemas and mobile projectionist units travelling through rural China, also increased radically.

In 1998 the Ministry of Culture revived mobile rural cinema through its 2131 Project. The project aimed to screen one movie per month in every village in rural China and to replace analog equipment with digital projectors.

The Chinese government does not count Chinese folk religion as a religion, because its boundaries are ambiguous and its structure poorly defined. Instead, it is considered part of China's cultural heritage. Buddhism and Taoism are recognized as the country's historical religions.

Revival of traditional religion in China has benefited from official interest in preserving traditional culture. Examples include Mazuism and the Sanyi teaching in Fujian, Yellow Emperor worship, and local worship of figures such as the Dragon King, Pangu or Caishen.

Harbin had a Jewish community of 13,000 in 1929. The Japanese occupation of Northeast China in 1931 and the establishment of Manchukuo in 1932 hurt it, as White Russian fascist elements engaged in antisemitism that Japanese authorities tolerated. Most of the Jews left for Tianjin, Shanghai and the British Mandate of Palestine.

culture.text: In 1949, Zhang Enpu, the 63rd Celestial Master of Taoism, escaped to Taiwan after the Republic of China government lost the Chinese Civil War. With him, the religious leadership and orthodoxy of Zhengyi Dao was brought to Taiwan.
